content:
The tile is a \(T\)-tetromino and covers \(4\) unit squares.

### 1. Area bound
The \(5\times4\) rectangle contains \(20\) squares, so at most
\[
\frac{20}{4}=5
\]
tiles could fit. If five fit, they would cover the rectangle completely.

### 2. Checkerboard coloring
Color the \(5\times4\) rectangle like a checkerboard. There are \(10\) squares of each color.

Every \(T\)-tile covers three squares of one color and one square of the other: the three squares in a line have colors \(B,W,B\), and the attached square has the same color as the two outer squares.

Thus each tile covers an odd number of black squares—either \(1\) or \(3\). Five tiles would therefore cover an odd total number of black squares, whereas the rectangle has \(10\) black squares. Hence five tiles cannot fit.

### 3. Four tiles are possible
The following arrangement places four tiles in the first four columns; dots represent unused squares:
\[
\begin{array}{ccccc}
A&A&A&B&\cdot\\
C&A&B&B&\cdot\\
C&C&D&B&\cdot\\
C&D&D&D&\cdot
\end{array}
\]
Each letter forms one \(T\)-tile.

Therefore, the maximum number of tiles is
\[
\boxed{4}.
\]
